analysis.one_liner: Protects workers' wages, severance, pensions, and union contracts when their employer goes bankrupt, and limits executive bonuses and clawbacks in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced on December 19, 2024 — fifteen days before the Congress ended — was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when that Congress expired.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company files for bankruptcy today, employees often stand behind lenders in line for unpaid wages, severance, and pension contributions, while courts can wipe out union contracts and executives can keep retention bonuses and exit pay. This bill would rewrite the bankruptcy code to fix that: it would double the protected wage amount to $20,000, give workers priority for severance and layoff-notice damages, require companies to keep paying retiree health benefits and to negotiate seriously before tearing up a union contract, and bar big executive bonuses and golden parachutes when workers take cuts. It would also let courts claw back executive pay and require buyers of a bankrupt company's assets to favor bids that preserve jobs.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees of companies that file for bankruptcy. They would collect up to $20,000 in back wages ahead of most creditors, gain priority claims for severance pay, pension contributions, and federal and state layoff-notice (WARN Act) damages, keep retiree health coverage unless a court finds cuts are truly unavoidable, and see unions get a real seat in the negotiation before a collective bargaining agreement is rejected. Retirees could claim pension shortfalls directly in bankruptcy, unions could file claims on members' behalf, and employees' 401(k) stock could be valued as of the case's start rather than its crashed value when the employer committed fraud. Courts would have to weigh job preservation when choosing among buyers of a company's assets, and executives of firms that cut worker benefits would face limits on bonuses, exit pay, and clawbacks of past compensation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees of bankrupt companies

how_it_helps.text: Raises the priority wage cap from $10,000 to $20,000 per worker and extends it to severance pay and to employee benefit plan contributions, so unpaid workers recover more before secured lenders take the collateral.
Gives bankruptcy priority to back pay, civil penalties, and damages owed under federal and state labor laws, including WARN Act layoff-notice violations.

Rewrites the rules for rejecting collective bargaining agreements and cutting retiree benefits: companies must negotiate in good faith first, cuts must be limited to the minimum needed to exit bankruptcy and cannot be disproportionate, courts must weigh alternatives from the union on clear and convincing evidence, and unions recover the fees of fighting the motion.

Requires courts approving asset sales or reorganization plans to give substantial weight to which bidder will preserve jobs, maintain pay and conditions, and assume pension and retiree health obligations — and to approve the bid that best does so.

Restricts executive pay in bankruptcy: end-of-case bonuses and retention pay must be part of a program generally applicable to all full-time employees, incentive pay is capped far below current law (2 times base compensation instead of 10, and 10 percent instead of 25 percent for equity transfers), and exit compensation is capped at the industry's 50th percentile and barred from being excessive compared to losses suffered by the nonmanagement workforce.

Bars special treatment for executives — deferred compensation and executive retiree benefit plans cannot be assumed if the company terminated its employee pension plan or cut worker or retiree health benefits — and allows the estate to claw back a proportional share of executive pay when workers' benefits were reduced, plus recover insider transfers made in the year before filing.

Treats unpaid post-filing wages, severance, and benefit contributions as costs of preserving the lender's collateral — overriding private waivers — so secured lenders cannot contract around paying workers first.

analysis.who_pays: Secured lenders and distressed-asset investors, who would recover less from failed companies' collateral; the executives and senior managers of bankrupt firms, who would lose retention bonuses, golden parachutes, and incentive plans and face clawbacks of past pay; and companies in distress, whose reorganizations would be slower and more expensive if unions and retirees gain leverage.

drawbacks.text: Raising worker priority claims and making lenders liable for unpaid wages and benefits could make loans to struggling companies riskier and more expensive, potentially pushing some troubled firms straight to liquidation rather than restructuring.

The tougher standards for rejecting a collective bargaining agreement — good-faith negotiation, minimum-savings limits, and a clear-and-convincing court standard — could make some reorganizations unworkable, leaving a judge unable to approve a deal the company needs to survive, which would cost jobs at the surviving firm.

The clawback provisions and compensation caps would add litigation and complexity to already lengthy bankruptcies, and the 50th-percentile pay cap could make it hard to keep management at companies that genuinely need continuity.
The bill was introduced with only days left in the session and just one cosponsor, so it never went through committee scrutiny or received a cost estimate or hearing record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers at failed companies, the gains are concrete and direct: more of their unpaid wages and severance get paid, union contracts and retiree benefits are much harder to strip, and executives can no longer enrich themselves while the workforce takes cuts. The main costs fall on lenders and executives, though some of that cost could pass through to future borrowers as tighter credit for distressed firms, and some reorganizations could tip into liquidation. It is a substantial transfer of leverage from creditors and management toward labor, and a bank of this scale would normally need committee review; it received none.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with two weeks left in the session, sat in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote, and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Representatives Jerrold Nadler (D-NY) and Lou Correa (D-CA) introduced the bill on December 19, 2024, the final month of the 118th Congress.
The House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and no further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever taken.
The bill's one cosponsor was a House Democrat, and no Republican supported it.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died without any vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives of bankrupt companies and the secured lenders and distressed-asset investors who fund them are better off: under current law they keep their retention bonuses, exit packages, and first claim on the company's assets, while unpaid workers and stripped retirees absorb the losses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Executives and lenders to failed companies

industries.industry: Executives and senior management of bankrupt companies
industries.note: The bill caps and bars retention bonuses, golden parachutes, and special incentive pay when workers face benefit cuts, and lets the estate claw back executive compensation. Its gain for executives under current law comes directly at the expense of workers and retirees in the same case.

Unpaid wages, severance, and benefit contributions would be charged against the lenders' collateral even over private waivers, and asset-sale rules would force lenders to accept bids that preserve jobs rather than maximize recovery. Their interest in maximizing collateral recovery runs directly against workers' claims.

Unions could file claims on members' behalf, grieve and arbitrate during bankruptcy, recover legal fees from the company, and gain a seat and a veto-like standard before a contract is rejected. Union members' wages and benefits rise with the union's.

industries.industry: Private equity and corporate acquirers of distressed assets
industries.note: Buyers of bankrupt companies' assets would have to preserve jobs and assume pension and retiree health obligations to win court approval, raising acquisition costs. Bidders offering job preservation would gain an edge over rivals offering more cash.
